task: Extract boky's existing extension↔WebSocket-relay↔MCP devtools bridge into a standalone, boky-free Chrome-control tool inside this repo, usable by any MCP-capable terminal AI coding tool (Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Claude Code) without a Claude account. First version: core page actions (navigate, getPageText, readPage, findElement, clickElement, typeText, captureTab) plus page console-log and network-request capture queryable from MCP tools. Works locally from this repo via a script + MCP config entry; not published. Boky itself keeps working unchanged.

analysis.objective: Extract boky's working extension↔WebSocket-relay↔MCP path into a standalone, boky-free Chrome-control tool in this repo that any MCP-capable terminal AI coding tool can point at to navigate, read, find, click, type, screenshot, and query page console logs and network requests of a real Chrome tab, with no Claude-account dependency.
analysis.successDefinition: Done means all of the following hold locally: (1) a separate unpacked MV3 extension (own manifest, own name, no boky domain/provider/session code) loads in any Chrome profile with no sign-in and connects out to the relay; (2) a standalone relay process starts from a repo script (not requiring boky's nest-host WorkflowEngineModule) and routes command / command-response / observation frames between one extension and N controllers; (3) a stdio MCP server exposes a generic tool set — at minimum navigate, getPageText, readPage, findElement, clickElement, typeText, captureTab, plus readConsoleMessages and readNetworkRequests (queryable ring buffer, with a clear-since/limit parameter) — and none of boky's provider/session/storage probes; (4) a single MCP config snippet (command + args) documented in the tool's README works unchanged for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and Cursor agent, verified by hand with at least two of them; (5) a mechanical parity check asserts MCP-advertised actions == extension command handler cases, mirroring today's check-command-parity; (6) tsc --noEmit, eslint --max-warnings 0, and vitest pass for the new code with unit tests for the frame protocol/ring buffers and integration tests for relay routing and the MCP tool dispatch; (7) boky's existing extension, bridge, and verify pipeline keep passing unchanged.
assumptions: The tool lives in this repo as a new top-level package (e.g. tools/chrome-bridge/ with extension/, relay/, mcp/ subfolders), built with the same pnpm/vite/tsc/eslint/vitest toolchain, so the repo's existing gates apply without new CI plumbing.
'Extract' means copy-and-generalize into the new package; boky's own extension, BridgeRelayModule, and extension-mcp.mjs keep working as-is and are not migrated onto the new tool in this horizon.

The relay's existing 7-kind frame protocol (hello/role, command, command-response keyed by msg.data.id, observation broadcast to controllers, dashboard-* kinds) is already payload-opaque and boky-free; the extracted relay keeps command/command-response/observation and drops the dashboard-* kinds.

Page console logs are captured by a MAIN-world content script that wraps console.* and window error/unhandledrejection and relays entries to the service worker via chrome.runtime messaging (the same CSP-safe sink pattern log-forwarder.ts already uses); boky's current log-forwarder only captures the extension's own console, so page-console capture is new code modeled on it.

Network requests are captured by a MAIN-world fetch/XHR wrapper (the page-world-sniffer pattern) recording method, URL, status, timing and bounded body previews — not via chrome.debugger — because that path already exists in boky and does not trigger the 'extension is debugging this browser' banner.

Console and network entries are stored per tab in bounded in-memory ring buffers in the service worker and exposed as pull-style MCP tools (readConsoleMessages / readNetworkRequests with optional since/limit/filter); push streaming over MCP is not required for 'queryable by the calling tool'.
Commands target the currently active tab of the connected Chrome window, exactly as boky's commands do today; explicit tabId targeting is the deferred tab-management feature.
The relay listens on a configurable port defaulting to a port distinct from boky's 8765 so both can run simultaneously on the same machine.
One extension instance per relay is the supported topology; multiple Chrome profiles each need their own relay port (a documented limitation, not a feature).
Manifest permissions stay at tabs, activeTab, scripting, storage plus <all_urls> host permissions and MAIN/ISOLATED-world content scripts — the same set boky already ships.
risks: Boky's command handler, bridge client, messaging types and devtools domain types are interleaved with story/provider/session code; a naive copy drags in domain imports and ESLint layer rules (import/no-restricted-paths, chrome.* zones) will reject them — extraction must cut at the messaging/command boundary, not at the file level.

MAIN-world console/fetch wrapping runs at document_start on every site; sites with strict CSP, frozen console objects, or their own fetch monkey-patching may silently miss entries — capture fidelity will be best-effort and must be documented, not assumed complete.

Body capture on network requests can be unbounded (streams, large JSON, binary); without hard size caps and per-tab buffer limits the service worker memory grows until MV3 kills it — buffers must be capped by count and bytes.

MV3 service workers are suspended after ~30s idle; the outbound WebSocket and in-memory ring buffers die with it — the extracted client must keep the keepalive (alarms) behavior boky already has, and callers must accept buffers are per-worker-lifetime.

Different MCP clients (Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor) vary in stdio handling, tool-schema strictness, and env propagation; a config verified only with Claude Code may fail elsewhere — success requires manual verification with at least two non-Claude clients.

The relay accepts any local WebSocket client as a controller with no auth; any local process can drive the user's browser — acceptable for a localhost dev tool but must bind to 127.0.0.1 only and be called out in the README rather than silently shipped.
readPage returns full outerHTML and captureTab returns a PNG; both can exceed MCP client message limits on large pages — responses need truncation/size parameters.

The dead-export gate and coverage guard (every export must be imported and named in a test) apply to the new package; scaffolding shared types without consumers will fail verify until the consuming phase lands.
outOfScope: Tab and profile management (list/create/close/switch tabs, targeting a tab by id, multi-profile discovery) — the user explicitly deferred it; commands act on the active tab only.
Migrating boky itself onto the extracted tool or deleting boky's existing devtools bridge — reuse by copy is the goal; rewiring boky is a separate refactor with its own blast radius.
Publishing as an npm package or Chrome Web Store listing — quality bar is 'works locally from this repo via a script'.
Authentication/authorization on the relay or MCP server beyond localhost binding — local dev tool; adding tokens is a follow-up once a remote use-case exists.

Push/streaming of console and network events into MCP clients (notifications, SSE transport) — pull-style queryable buffers satisfy the stated need; MCP notification support across clients is inconsistent.
Advanced automation primitives (keyboard shortcuts, drag, file upload, form_input helpers, JavaScript eval, GIF recording, window resize) — beyond the core page actions the user listed.
Capturing network traffic via chrome.debugger / CDP or WebSocket frame capture — the fetch/XHR page-world wrapper covers the stated need without the debugger banner; CDP is a different architecture.
Persisting console/network history across service-worker restarts (IndexedDB) — in-memory ring buffers are sufficient for an interactive debugging loop.
Cross-browser support (Firefox, Safari, Edge-specific) — the extension is MV3 Chrome-first like boky.
A GUI/dashboard for the tool — consumers are terminal AI tools over MCP; no React UI is carried over.
analysis.domainShapeReason: The task is developer tooling machinery — extracting and generalizing a Chrome extension, a WebSocket relay, and an MCP stdio server — with no business entities or rules a domain expert would recognize.

ubiquitousLanguage.meaning: The standalone MV3 Chrome extension (service worker + content scripts) that executes commands in the browser and captures page events; connects outbound to the Relay.
The standalone local WebSocket server that routes frames between one connected Extension and any number of Controllers; opaque to payloads.
Any process (the MCP server, a log tailer, a test) that connects to the Relay with role=controller to send Commands and receive Observations.
The stdio Model Context Protocol server that terminal AI coding tools launch; it is a Controller that exposes Commands and buffer queries as MCP tools.
A request frame {id, action, params} sent Controller→Extension and its matching reply frame keyed by the same id.
A fire-and-forget frame Extension→Controllers carrying a captured event (console entry, network entry, extension log).
MAIN-world content script that wraps console.* and fetch/XHR in the page and relays entries to the service worker.
Bounded per-tab in-memory store of console and network entries in the service worker, queried by readConsoleMessages / readNetworkRequests.

discoveryFindings.finding: The MCP server is a single 241-line plain-JS ESM file using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk low-level `Server` + `StdioServerTransport` with `ListToolsRequestSchema`/`CallToolRequestSchema` handlers (not the high-level McpServer/zod API). It exposes exactly ONE tool, `ext_command`, whose inputSchema is `{action: enum(ACTIONS), params: object}` — not one MCP tool per action. Server identity is hardcoded `name: "book-story-extension"`.
discoveryFindings.implication: The success criterion 'MCP server exposes a generic tool set — navigate, getPageText, …' is a NEW shape, not a copy: today's server is a single dispatcher tool. Plan a phase that decides one-tool-with-enum vs N-discrete-tools; N discrete tools is safer across Codex/Gemini/Cursor whose enum handling varies, but it breaks the existing parity-check shape (see parity finding).

discoveryFindings.finding: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` (^1.0.0) and `ws` (^8.18.0) are declared in extension/package.json devDependencies, and extension/ is its own pnpm project (extension/pnpm-workspace.yaml, extension/pnpm-lock.yaml). The MCP file is `.mjs` — deliberately outside tsconfig and ESLint-typechecking (eslint.config.mjs has a `files: ["devtools/**/*.mjs"]` relaxed override) and excluded from vitest (`exclude: ["devtools/**"]`).
discoveryFindings.implication: Nothing in devtools/ is currently typechecked, linted-strictly, or tested. The task's gate requirement (tsc --noEmit + eslint --max-warnings 0 + vitest for the new code) means the new package cannot be a straight .mjs copy — it must be authored in TS with its own tsconfig/eslint/vitest, which is new plumbing, not inherited.

discoveryFindings.finding: BridgeClient in extension-mcp.mjs: hardcoded `const BRIDGE_URL = "ws://localhost:8765"` (no env override, unlike tail-logs.mjs which honors `BRIDGE_URL`), sends `{kind:"hello", role:"controller"}` on open, correlates by a monotonic integer `nextId` stored in a `pending` Map keyed by `msg.data.id`, hardcoded 30s per-command timeout, exponential reconnect 1s→15s cap, and rejects all pending on close with 'Bridge connection lost'.
discoveryFindings.implication: The correlation/timeout/reconnect logic is small and directly portable, but the URL must become env/arg-configurable (`--port`/`CHROME_BRIDGE_URL`) for the new default port. Integer ids from multiple controllers collide at the relay for `command` frames (see relay finding) — worth ids being uuid/prefixed in the extracted client.

discoveryFindings.finding: BridgeRelayService is a Nest `@Injectable` with `OnApplicationBootstrap`/`OnModuleDestroy`, creating a raw `new WebSocketServer({ port })` from the `ws` package. It handles 7 frame kinds: hello, observation, command, command-response, dashboard-request, dashboard-response, dashboard-broadcast. Role is fixed on the first `hello` (`role === "extension" ? extensions : controllers`; anything not literally "extension" becomes a controller). Malformed JSON and unknown kinds are silently dropped.
discoveryFindings.implication: Confirms the stage1 assumption: routing is payload-opaque and boky-free. The extracted relay is a ~120-line dependency-free `ws` script (drop the 3 dashboard-* kinds and the pendingDashboardRequests/nextRelayRequestId machinery entirely) — no Nest, no ConfigService, no module extraction from nest-host needed.

discoveryFindings.finding: `new WebSocketServer({ port: this.port })` passes NO `host`, so `ws` binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0), not 127.0.0.1. Port default is `DEFAULT_RELAY_PORT = 8765`, overridable only via the Nest ConfigService key `NEST_BRIDGE_PORT` (zod schema, `services/nest-host/src/config/env.schema.ts`, default 8765).
discoveryFindings.implication: The stage1 risk 'must bind to 127.0.0.1 only' is a real behavioral CHANGE, not a carry-over — the extracted relay must explicitly pass `{ host: "127.0.0.1", port }`. Also note boky's relay will keep occupying 8765 on all interfaces, so the new default port must differ (e.g. 8766).

discoveryFindings.finding: BridgeRelayModule itself is trivial (`providers/exports: [BridgeRelayService]`, no imports) but the service constructor-injects `ConfigService`, and it is only ever started via `AppModule` → `main.ts` `bootstrap()`, which also boots WorkflowEngineModule, RedisStreamModule (ioredis), MongoModule (mongodb), InteractiveWorkflowModule and an Express HTTP listener on 3000. Root `npm start` = `npm --prefix services/nest-host run start` = the whole app.
discoveryFindings.implication: Confirms the assumption that the relay cannot be started today without the full Nest app (Redis/Mongo included). Reimplementing the relay standalone is correct and far cheaper than trying to boot BridgeRelayModule in isolation; no refactor of nest-host is needed.

discoveryFindings.finding: The extension side is module-level singleton state (`let socket`, `outbox`, `commandHandler`) in bridge-client.ts, hardcoded `ws://localhost:8765`, 2000ms fixed reconnect, lazy dial-on-first-use, with an outbox that buffers observations until open. It imports its wire types from `../../../devtools/domain/types.js` (a relative reach OUT of src/ into devtools/) and imports `isBroadcastEnvelope`/`isMessageEnvelope` + `MessageTransport` from `../messaging/` for the dashboard-request path.
discoveryFindings.implication: Extraction cut line: keep hello/observation/command/command-response, delete the entire dashboard-request/dashboard-response/broadcast half — that half is the only thing pulling in boky's messaging layer. Port becomes configurable; wire types get co-located in the new package instead of a cross-tree relative import.

discoveryFindings.finding: Keepalive is a separate module using `chrome.alarms.create("bridge-keepalive", { periodInMinutes: 0.5 })` with a no-op listener; the alarm firing itself resets the MV3 idle timer and bridge-client's own timer reconnects. It has an `AlarmsPort` interface for injection and an idempotency guard + `resetBridgeKeepaliveForTests`.
discoveryFindings.implication: Fully boky-free and copyable verbatim (~40 lines). Requires `alarms` in the new manifest's permissions — note boky's manifest lists alarms, which stage1's assumed permission set (tabs/activeTab/scripting/storage) omits. Add `alarms`.

discoveryFindings.finding: The `switch` over action names lives in `handleCommand()` in src/background/command-handler.ts (~line 233-485), 20 cases. Handlers are behind a `CommandHandlerPorts` interface; the chrome-specific implementations live in `chromeCommandHandlerPorts(providerRegistry, sessionStore, router, macroDeps)` in the same file. Only 7 of 20 cases are the target generic page actions; the other 13 (getStorage/setStorage/mutateStorage/getProviderState(Live)/getSessionState/reloadActiveTab/reloadExtension/simulateProviderEvent/readSelectorText/probeProviderRouter/probeSendNewMessageMacro/ping) are boky-specific or dev-only.
discoveryFindings.implication: Confirms the stage1 risk: this file's imports pull in providers, session, ProviderRouter, ProviderId and provider-macros. The extraction must copy only the 7 page-action cases + the ports pattern, not the file — roughly 200 lines of the 760. `ping` is worth keeping as a health check.

discoveryFindings.finding: All page actions are `chrome.scripting.executeScript({target:{tabId}, func, args})` from the service worker — NO content-script messaging: readPage = `document.documentElement.outerHTML`; getPageText = `document.body.innerText`; findElement = `querySelectorAll(sel).length` → `{found, matches}`; clickElement = `el.click()` on HTMLElement; typeText = sets `.value` + dispatches input/change (or `textContent` + input for contentEditable); navigateTo = `chrome.tabs.update(tabId,{url})`; captureTab = `chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab(windowId,{format:"png"})`. Target tab comes from `chrome.tabs.query({active:true,currentWindow:true})`; captureTab uses `tab.windowId`, the rest `tab.id`.
discoveryFindings.implication: These 7 implementations are already boky-free and copy verbatim. None of them truncate output — readPage returns full outerHTML and captureTab a full PNG dataUrl, so the stage1 truncation risk requires NEW code (maxBytes/maxChars params) at either the port or the MCP layer.

discoveryFindings.finding: `extension/devtools/domain/types.ts` (153 lines) is the shared protocol module: `BridgeMessage` union (7 kinds), `Command {id, action, params}`, `CommandResponse {id, result?, error?}`, `Observation` union with types log|error|network|dom-error|runtime-error and `ObservationSource = "service-worker" | "content-script"`, plus per-command param/result interfaces (FindElementParams, TypeTextParams, CaptureTabResult, …). `KnownCommandAction` duplicates the ACTIONS list a third time.
discoveryFindings.implication: This is the cleanest extraction seed — a boky-free protocol module the new package can copy and trim (drop dashboard-* kinds and the 13 boky actions). Note `ObservationSource` has no `page` variant, so page-world console/network capture needs a new source value.

discoveryFindings.finding: check-command-parity.mjs is 53 lines of regex: it greps `case "X":` out of `../src/background/command-handler.ts` and `const ACTIONS = [...]` out of extension-mcp.mjs, diffs the two sets, exits 1 on drift. It is wired as `devtools:check-parity` inside extension's `verify:fast` script — but NOT into root scripts/verify.sh.
discoveryFindings.implication: The 'mechanical parity check' criterion is a ~50-line regex script to mirror with new paths — cheap. But note the third list (`KnownCommandAction` in types.ts) is NOT covered today; the new package should either derive all lists from one const array or extend the check to 3 sources. Also decide where to hook it: root verify.sh has no per-package extension point (stages are a hardcoded array).

discoveryFindings.finding: log-forwarder.ts patches console.log/error and global error/unhandledrejection in the SERVICE WORKER and in boky's ISOLATED content script — it captures the EXTENSION's own console, never the page's. Its doc comment explicitly warns that a content script must pass a `sink` relaying over chrome.runtime (`bridge/observation` message type) because host-page `connect-src` CSP blocks a content-script WebSocket to ws://localhost.
discoveryFindings.implication: Confirms stage1: page-console capture is NEW code. The CSP note is load-bearing — the new MAIN-world capture must go page→content-script (postMessage) →service-worker (chrome.runtime) →WebSocket, never open a socket from the page/content world.

discoveryFindings.finding: The MAIN-world fetch/XHR/WebSocket interceptor exists as a TypeScript string literal (`pageWorldSnifferSource.source` in sniffer-source.ts) emitted by a custom Vite plugin as `dist/page-world-sniffer.js`, registered as `web_accessible_resources` AND patched into the BUILT manifest's content_scripts as `{world:"MAIN", run_at:"document_start"}` by the plugin's `closeBundle` (crx() cannot take a synthesized asset as a content_scripts entry in the source manifest). Idempotence-guarded via `window.__bokySnifferInstalled`.
discoveryFindings.implication: This is the single trickiest thing to reuse: the MAIN-world script cannot be a normal TS module under @crxjs. Budget a dedicated phase for the build plumbing. Consider dropping @crxjs entirely for the new extension (a plain vite multi-entry build + hand-written manifest listing a real MAIN-world file) — simpler than replicating the closeBundle hack.

discoveryFindings.finding: Page-world → content-script uses `window.postMessage` with a namespaced envelope: `PAGE_BRIDGE_NAMESPACE = "__boky_capture_v1__"` plus a `channel` discriminant. Two channels exist today: `PAGE_BRIDGE_CHANNEL = "raw-reply-frame"` (page-bridge.ts) and `NETWORK_ACTIVITY_CHANNEL = "network-activity-v1"` (network-activity-bridge.ts). Each has a validating type-guard predicate at the content-script trust boundary, and the recorder drops any message whose `event.source` is not the page's own window.
discoveryFindings.implication: The envelope+namespace+predicate pattern is the convention to copy (rename the namespace — it literally contains 'boky'). No CustomEvent path exists. Network frames already carry method/url/status shape via `network-activity-frame.ts`, worth reading as a schema seed for readNetworkRequests.

discoveryFindings.finding: No bounded ring-buffer / capped-collection utility exists in extension/src — the recorder path (network-activity-recorder.ts, conversation-recorder.ts, llm-capture-sink.ts) streams into provider-session log repositories, not into an in-memory capped store, and the bridge outbox is an unbounded array.
discoveryFindings.implication: Contrary to any assumption of reuse, the ring buffer for console/network entries is 100% new code. Good news for the gates: it is pure, dependency-free, and trivially unit-testable — a natural first phase that satisfies the 'unit tests for frame protocol/ring buffers' criterion.

discoveryFindings.finding: The source manifest is `extension/public/manifest.json`, MV3, permissions `[tabs, activeTab, scripting, storage, alarms]`, host_permissions `<all_urls>`, background `{service_worker: "src/background/service-worker.ts", type: "module"}` (a TS path — @crxjs compiles it), one ISOLATED content script at document_idle, an `action` with no popup, and `web_accessible_resources` for page-world-sniffer.js.
discoveryFindings.implication: Directly copyable as the new manifest baseline; add `alarms` to stage1's assumed permission list and drop the `action`/dashboard entry. Note the manifest points at TS sources, which only works under @crxjs — a non-crx build needs built JS paths instead.

discoveryFindings.finding: Three vite configs exist: vite.config.ts (crx extension build → dist/), vite.standalone.config.ts and vite.qa.config.ts (Vite DEV SERVERS for the React dashboard / QA harness at e.g. localhost:5175, run via `dev:standalone`/`dev:qa`), outputting dist-standalone/ and dist-qa/. Only vite.config.ts builds the extension.
discoveryFindings.implication: The multi-config precedent is for dev servers, not multiple extension entrypoints — it does not give the new package a pattern for building extension + relay + MCP together. Expect: one vite config for the new extension, plain `tsc` for relay+MCP node code.

discoveryFindings.finding: The root is NOT a workspace of any kind — root package.json has no `workspaces` field, uses npm (package-lock.json) and `"type": "commonjs"`. Cross-package invocation is by explicit prefix: `npm --prefix services/nest-host run build`, `pnpm -C extension run typecheck`. extension/ and services/nest-host/ are independent installs (extension uses pnpm with its own pnpm-workspace.yaml + pnpm-lock; nest-host uses npm with package-lock).
discoveryFindings.implication: Refutes the stage1 assumption 'built with the same pnpm toolchain so existing gates apply without new CI plumbing.' A new `tools/chrome-bridge/` package gets its OWN package.json + lockfile + tsconfig + eslint.config + vitest.config and must be wired into root verify.sh by hand — treat this as an explicit setup phase, not free.

discoveryFindings.finding: scripts/verify.sh is a hardcoded 9-stage array, and EVERY stage is scoped to extension/ or to root hooks: typecheck/lint/tests all run `pnpm -C extension`, dead-code runs `./scripts/block-dead-code.sh --all`, security runs `pnpm -C extension audit`. `services/nest-host` is not in verify.sh at all despite having its own tsconfig/eslint/vitest and its own `build`/`lint`/`typecheck`/`test:unit`/`test:int` scripts.
discoveryFindings.implication: There is precedent for a second package living OUTSIDE the root verify pipeline (nest-host). The plan can either follow that precedent (self-contained `tools/chrome-bridge` with its own verify script) or add stages — following precedent is lower risk and keeps 'boky's verify pipeline passes unchanged' trivially true.

discoveryFindings.finding: The dead-export hook hardcodes `SRC_ROOT = existsSync('extension/src') ? 'extension/src' : 'src'` and walks only that tree; `block-dead-code.sh --all` therefore only ever scans extension/src. It also carries a `DEFERRED_EXPORTS` allowlist keyed by `path:symbolName` for intentionally-unwired exports.
discoveryFindings.implication: Refutes the stage1 risk 'the dead-export gate applies to the new package' — it does NOT reach outside extension/src, so scaffolding unconsumed shared types in tools/ will not trip it. Don't budget DEFERRED_EXPORTS bookkeeping unless the new code lands inside extension/src.

discoveryFindings.finding: .testguard.json rules are anchored `^extension/src/...` for the three specific levels, but the final catch-all rule is `{ "match": ".*", "suffix": ".unit.test.ts", "level": "unit" }` with `requireSymbolMentions: true`, and testLocations `{dir}/{base}{suffix}` or `tests/{base}{suffix}`. The ignore list covers index.ts, types.ts, ports.ts, *.d.ts, __fixtures__, *.config.ts.
discoveryFindings.implication: The catch-all DOES reach files outside extension/ (check-tests.mjs runs on changed files repo-wide), so every new .ts file in tools/ needs a co-located `.unit.test.ts` naming its exported symbols — unless the file is named index.ts/types.ts/ports.ts. Name the protocol module `types.ts` to inherit the ignore, or plan tests for it.

discoveryFindings.finding: extension/eslint.config.mjs (~330 lines) layers strictTypeChecked over `**/*.ts`, defines import/no-restricted-paths zones (inward-only), bans `chrome`/@types/chrome imports and DOM+chrome lib types in `src/domain/**`, and bans raw `chrome.runtime.sendMessage`/`onMessage`/`chrome.tabs.sendMessage`/`chrome.runtime.connect` repo-wide via no-restricted-syntax selectors (only chrome-transport.ts is exempt). `devtools/**/*.mjs` gets a relaxed override.
discoveryFindings.implication: Confirms the stage1 risk. The raw-chrome-messaging ban would force the new page→SW messaging through a typed transport wrapper IF the code lived under extension/. A separate tools/ package with its own eslint.config.mjs escapes these selectors — another argument for the standalone package with a lighter, purpose-built config.

discoveryFindings.finding: Root `.mcp.json` registers one stdio server `extension-bridge` with an ABSOLUTE path (`/Users/dimitrykatz/workspace/boky/extension/devtools/extension-mcp.mjs`), and extension/mcp.json duplicates it with a relative path. Additionally, `extension/scripts/register-mcp.mjs` already exists and registers the same server into gemini, qwen and crush CLIs (`--targets`, `--scope`, `--dry-run` flags), noting Claude Code needs no entry because it reads .mcp.json.
discoveryFindings.implication: Significant unexpected asset: the 'one config snippet works across CLIs' criterion has a working precedent script to copy/parameterize for the new server — and it proves gemini/qwen/crush config shapes were already reverse-engineered. Also: the absolute path in .mcp.json means the new entry should use a repo-relative launcher script to stay portable.

discoveryFindings.finding: tail-logs.mjs is a 60-line controller: connects, sends hello/controller, prints observations via `summarizeObservation` from format-observation.mjs, and if stdin is piped treats the JSON as a one-shot command then exits on the command-response. It honors `BRIDGE_URL` env, and its error message tells the user to run `npm start` at the repo root.
discoveryFindings.implication: A ready-made template for the new tool's manual smoke-test/debug CLI, and the natural harness for the integration tests of relay routing without needing a real Chrome.

discoveryFindings.finding: There is no `tools/` or `packages/` directory; the only non-extension package is `services/nest-host` (Nest, npm, own tsconfig/eslint/vitest/README, per-package CLAUDE.md, excluded from root verify.sh). Every module folder carries a CLAUDE.md; docs/roadmaps/ holds triples of `<name>-roadmap.json` / `.md` / `.status.json` plus per-project subfolders, with in-progress analysis under docs/roadmaps/.tmp/<slug>/.
discoveryFindings.implication: Creating a new top-level `tools/chrome-bridge/` is a new-but-consistent move; follow the nest-host precedent (self-contained package + README + CLAUDE.md files per folder) and the docs/roadmaps triple naming for the roadmap artifacts.

phases.name: Add standalone package with protocol types
phases.goal: Create the new self-contained package `tools/chrome-bridge/` (own package.json, tsconfig, ESLint flat config, vitest config, `npm run verify` = typecheck + lint + test) and ship its first real module: the wire protocol shared by every later phase — the WebSocket frame types (`hello`, `command`, `command-response`, `observation`) and a single `PAGE_ACTIONS` const array (`ping`, `navigateTo`, `getPageText`, `readPage`, `findElement`, `clickElement`, `typeText`, `captureTab`) with per-action param/result types, compiled and covered by a passing unit test.
phases.rationale: Discovery showed the repo root is not a workspace and nothing (tsconfig, ESLint, vitest, dependencies) is inherited by a new top-level folder, and the existing devtools code is untyped .mjs that is neither typechecked nor tested. Every later phase (relay, extension, controller, MCP server) imports the same frame and action types, so the shared protocol module plus the toolchain that compiles it must exist first.

phases.name: Add standalone WebSocket relay process
phases.goal: Implement the Relay — a dependency-light local WebSocket server (only the `ws` package) that accepts one Extension and any number of Controllers, identifies each socket by its first `hello` frame, forwards `command` frames from controllers to the extension, forwards `command-response` frames back to every controller, and broadcasts `observation` frames from the extension to all controllers — started by `npm run relay` and bound to 127.0.0.1 on port 8766 (env `CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT` overrides).
phases.rationale: Today the relay only exists as a NestJS service that cannot start without the whole nest-host app (Redis, Mongo, workflow engine), and it binds every network interface on port 8765. The standalone tool needs a relay any developer can start with one script, that binds localhost only, and that does not collide with boky's relay when both run.
changes: Add `ws` (+ `@types/ws`) to the package dependencies.

Create `src/relay/relay.ts` exporting `startRelay({ host, port }): Promise<{ port, close(): Promise<void> }>` — port from `new WebSocketServer({ host: '127.0.0.1', port })`; explicitly pass `host` (boky's relay omits it and therefore listens on 0.0.0.0). Port the routing from `services/nest-host/src/bridge-relay/bridge-relay.service.ts`: role fixed by the first `hello` frame (`role === 'extension'` → extensions set, anything else → controllers set); `command` → all extension sockets; `command-response` and `observation` → all controller sockets; parse incoming text with `JSON.parse` → `unknown` → a hand-written frame type guard from the protocol module (no `as` casts); silently drop malformed JSON and unknown kinds; remove sockets from their set on close. Drop the three `dashboard-*` kinds and the pending-request machinery entirely.

Create `src/relay/main.ts` (the process entry): read `CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT` (default 8766), call `startRelay`, log `chrome-bridge relay listening on ws://127.0.0.1:<port>`; add `"relay": "tsx src/relay/main.ts"` (or `node dist/relay/main.js` after `tsc` build — pick one; same convention the MCP server phase in this horizon will reuse) to package.json scripts.

Write `relay.unit.test.ts` that starts the relay on port 0 (ephemeral), connects a fake extension socket and two controller sockets with real `ws` clients, and asserts: a `command` from controller A reaches the extension and not controller B; a `command-response` from the extension reaches both controllers; an `observation` reaches both controllers; a malformed frame is dropped without killing the connection; `close()` shuts the server down. Use event promises, no sleeps.
inputs: services/nest-host/src/bridge-relay/bridge-relay.service.ts (routing logic to port, minus dashboard kinds)
phases.expectedResult: `tools/chrome-bridge/src/relay/relay.ts` with a passing routing test; `npm run relay` prints the listening line on ws://127.0.0.1:8766.

rubric.label: Frame routing matches the role-based fan-out contract
rubric.ruleStatement: Given one extension socket and N controller sockets identified by their first `hello` frame, `command` frames go only to extension sockets, and `command-response` plus `observation` frames go to every controller socket and never back to the extension. 10: the test suite covers both directions plus the no-echo cases and a late-joining controller; 8: the three happy paths are asserted with real `ws` clients; below 7: any direction is untested or a frame leaks to the wrong role.
passCriteria: `tools/chrome-bridge/src/relay/relay.unit.test.ts` starts the relay on port 0 and connects one fake extension socket and at least two controller sockets using the real `ws` client, each sending a `hello` frame first.

A `command` sent by controller A is asserted to arrive at the extension socket AND asserted NOT to arrive at controller B (the negative assertion is present, e.g. a message listener on B that fails the test or a bounded 'no message' check via a resolved competing promise).
A `command-response` and an `observation` sent by the extension are each asserted to arrive at both controllers, and asserted NOT to be echoed back to the extension socket.
A controller that connects after the extension has already sent frames still receives subsequent `observation` frames (late-join case).
A socket that sends a data frame before any `hello` frame is either ignored or treated per the documented default, and the test states which; it does not crash the server.
failureExamples: The test asserts controller A's command reaches the extension but never asserts controller B did not receive it — a relay that broadcasts every frame to every socket passes the suite.
`command-response` is forwarded to all sockets including the extension, so the extension receives its own reply back; no test catches it because only controller-side listeners are attached.

Role is decided by the socket's most recent `hello` instead of its first, so a controller that later sends `hello` with role extension silently becomes an extension; test only sends one hello per socket so this passes unnoticed.
A frame arriving before `hello` throws inside the message handler and closes that socket because the role lookup returns undefined.

rubric.label: Malformed and unknown frames are dropped without harming the connection or server
rubric.ruleStatement: Non-JSON text, JSON that fails the frame type guard, unknown `kind` values, and binary frames are silently discarded; the sending socket stays open and other sockets keep receiving traffic. Parsing goes `JSON.parse` -> `unknown` -> hand-written guard with no `as` casts. 10: all four malformed classes are tested and a subsequent valid frame on the same socket still routes; 8: non-JSON and unknown-kind are tested with the socket verified open afterwards; below 7: a malformed frame can throw out of the `message` handler or the guard uses casts.
passCriteria: After a controller sends the literal text `not json{`, the test asserts that socket's `readyState` is still OPEN and that a following valid `command` from the same socket still reaches the extension.

A well-formed JSON object with an unrecognized `kind` (e.g. `{"kind":"dashboard-state"}`) and a JSON object missing required fields (e.g. `{"kind":"command"}` with no `data`) are both dropped: no socket receives them and no process-level `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` fires during the test (attach a listener that fails the test).

`grep -n ' as ' tools/chrome-bridge/src/relay/relay.ts` shows no type assertions on the parsed message; the parse result is typed `unknown` and narrowed by the guard imported from the protocol module.
Sending a binary frame (a `Buffer`) does not close the socket or throw; the test either covers it or the code path visibly treats non-string data as a drop.
failureExamples: `JSON.parse` is wrapped in try/catch but the type guard is only applied to `kind`; a `command` frame with `data: null` passes the guard and the forward code dereferences `data.id`, throwing inside the `ws` message listener and emitting an unhandled error event that closes the socket.

The `message` handler calls `raw.toString()` on every frame, so a binary frame is parsed as garbage bytes and silently works — but a `ws` frame with `isBinary=true` carrying valid JSON is forwarded as text, breaking clients that expect binary passthrough; no test covers binary at all.
The guard is written as `(m as Frame).kind === 'command'` to satisfy the compiler, which lint rejects under `no-restricted-syntax`.
Malformed frames are logged with `console.error` including the full payload, so a flood of garbage from one controller spams the relay's stdout and hides the listening line.

rubric.label: Relay binds 127.0.0.1 only on a configurable port that defaults to 8766
rubric.ruleStatement: The server is created with an explicit `host: '127.0.0.1'` so it is not reachable on other interfaces, the port defaults to 8766 and is overridden by `CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT`, and a non-numeric or out-of-range env value fails loudly instead of silently falling back. 10: bind address is asserted in a test and invalid env is rejected with a clear message; 8: the explicit host is in code and default/override behaviour is shown by the log line; below 7: the host option is omitted (inherits 0.0.0.0) or the port is hard-coded.
passCriteria: `tools/chrome-bridge/src/relay/relay.ts` passes `host` explicitly into `new WebSocketServer({ host, port })`; the `main.ts` entry passes `'127.0.0.1'`.

Running `npm run relay` (from `tools/chrome-bridge`) prints exactly `chrome-bridge relay listening on ws://127.0.0.1:8766`; running `CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT=8799 npm run relay` prints the same line with 8799.
With the relay running, `lsof -nP -iTCP:8766 -sTCP:LISTEN` (or `netstat -an`) shows the listener on `127.0.0.1:8766`, not `*:8766` or `0.0.0.0:8766`.
The unit test reads the ephemeral port back from the `startRelay` result (`address().port`) rather than assuming a fixed number, and the returned `port` field equals what the server actually bound.
`CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT=abc npm run relay` exits non-zero with a message naming the variable, rather than starting on NaN/8766.
failureExamples: `startRelay` accepts `host` in its options type but `main.ts` calls `startRelay({ port })`, so the `ws` server defaults to all interfaces exactly like boky's relay; the log line still says 127.0.0.1 so nobody notices.
`Number(process.env.CHROME_BRIDGE_PORT ?? 8766)` yields `NaN` for a typo, `ws` treats NaN as port 0, and the relay starts on a random port while the log line prints `ws://127.0.0.1:NaN`.

The port is resolved once at module import time in `relay.ts`, so the test cannot pass port 0 without also setting the env var, and the test suite therefore pins a fixed port that collides when vitest runs files in parallel.
The returned `port` is the requested value, not `server.address().port`, so with port 0 it returns 0 and the test has to reach into internals to find the real port.

rubric.label: Start/close lifecycle is clean and repeatable
rubric.ruleStatement: `startRelay` resolves only after the server is actually listening, rejects if the port is already taken, and `close()` terminates every connected socket, releases the port, and resolves; the socket sets shrink on client disconnect so no dead sockets are written to. 10: start-fails-on-busy-port, socket-set cleanup after client disconnect, and close-then-restart on the same port are all tested; 8: close resolves and the port is reusable in a test; below 7: `close()` resolves before the port is free or a closed client socket is still targeted by forwarding.
passCriteria: A test calls `startRelay({ host, port: 0 })`, then `close()`, then `startRelay` again on the port the first instance reported, and the second start succeeds (proves the listener was released, not just `wss.close()` with hanging clients).
A test starts two relays on the same explicit port; the second `startRelay` call rejects (does not hang or resolve) with the `EADDRINUSE` error surfaced.

After a controller disconnects, a subsequent `observation` from the extension does not throw and the relay does not attempt `send` on the closed socket (assert via an `error` listener on the process or by inspecting that no `ws` 'WebSocket is not open' error is emitted).

`close()` returns a Promise that resolves after all client sockets have emitted `close` on the client side — the test awaits both the server promise and the client `close` events without a timeout-based sleep.
The vitest file has no `setTimeout`-based waits and finishes in under a few seconds; every wait is an event promise (`once(ws, 'open')`, message promises).
failureExamples: `startRelay` resolves synchronously after constructing `WebSocketServer` without awaiting the `listening` event, so a test connecting immediately gets `ECONNREFUSED` intermittently under load.

`close()` calls `wss.close(cb)` only; per `ws` semantics the callback fires only after all clients disconnect, so with a still-connected fake extension the promise never resolves and the test hits the vitest timeout.
Sockets are removed from the role set on `close` but not on `error`, so a client that dies abruptly stays in the set and the next `command` forward throws 'WebSocket is not open'.
A busy-port `error` event on the `WebSocketServer` is not wired to the start promise's reject, so `startRelay` on a taken port hangs forever.

phases.name: Add standalone extension executing page actions
phases.goal: Create the standalone MV3 extension (own manifest named 'Chrome Bridge', no boky code) whose service worker dials the Relay at ws://127.0.0.1:8766 on startup, sends `hello role=extension`, keeps the MV3 service worker alive with a `chrome.alarms` heartbeat, reconnects on a fixed delay, and dispatches every incoming `command` frame to a real handler for each of the eight `PAGE_ACTIONS` — `ping`, `navigateTo`, `getPageText`, `readPage`, `findElement`, `clickElement`, `typeText`, `captureTab` — acting on the active tab of the current window via `chrome.scripting.executeScript` / `chrome.tabs`, with an optional `maxChars` truncation on `readPage`/`getPageText` (default 200 000 characters, response reports `truncated: true`), replying with a matching `command-response`; built by Vite into a loadable `dist/extension/` folder.
phases.rationale: The browser side of the bridge is currently a service worker entangled with boky's providers, sessions, and dashboard messaging, hardcoded to boky's port, and the eight page actions a terminal AI tool needs already have working boky-free implementations buried in a file full of boky-specific commands. A clean extension that loads unpacked in any Chrome profile, proves the connection loop (connect, keepalive, reconnect, request/response correlation), and answers all eight actions from day one means there is no intermediate build with unusable stub handlers. Copying only those handlers behind a small chrome-API port makes them unit-testable with fakes and keeps large page HTML from overflowing MCP client message limits.
changes: Create `extension/manifest.json` (hand-written, MV3) from `extension/public/manifest.json`: name 'Chrome Bridge', permissions `[tabs, activeTab, scripting, storage, alarms]`, host_permissions `<all_urls>`, background `{ service_worker: 'service-worker.js', type: 'module' }` (a BUILT JS path — no @crxjs). No `action`, no content scripts, no web_accessible_resources in this horizon.

Create `vite.extension.config.ts`: plain Vite build (no @crxjs) with rollup input `src/extension/service-worker.ts`, output `dist/extension/service-worker.js` as a single ES bundle, and a copy of `extension/manifest.json` into `dist/extension/` (vite-plugin-static-copy or a 10-line closeBundle hook). Add `"build:extension": "vite build -c vite.extension.config.ts"` to package.json; add `@types/chrome` and `vite` devDependencies.

Create `src/extension/bridge-client.ts` by porting `extension/src/infrastructure/bridge/bridge-client.ts` and cutting the dashboard-request/response/broadcast half (the only part that imports boky's messaging layer): `createBridgeClient({ url, socketFactory, onCommand, reconnectDelayMs })` that dials eagerly (not lazily on first use — the standalone extension has nothing else to trigger a dial), sends `hello role=extension` on open, parses frames via the protocol type guard, calls `onCommand(command)` and sends the returned `CommandResponse`, buffers outbound frames in a bounded outbox until open, and reconnects after a fixed 2000ms delay. Default URL constant `ws://127.0.0.1:8766`.

Copy `extension/src/infrastructure/bridge/keepalive.ts` verbatim (it is boky-free) as `src/extension/keepalive.ts`: `chrome.alarms.create('bridge-keepalive', { periodInMinutes: 0.5 })` with the injectable `AlarmsPort` and idempotency guard.

Create `src/extension/command-dispatch.ts`: `createCommandDispatcher(handlers: Record<PageAction, Handler>)` returning `(command) => Promise<CommandResponse>`; unknown action → `{ id, error: 'unknown action <x>' }`; thrown handler errors → `{ id, error: message }`. Typing the handler map as `Record<PageAction, Handler>` means the compiler refuses to build if an action from `PAGE_ACTIONS` has no handler — this is the mechanical parity check for the extension side.

Create `src/extension/chrome-ports.ts`: a narrow `ChromePorts` interface `{ queryActiveTab(): Promise<{ id, windowId }>, executeScript<T>(tabId, func, args): Promise<T>, updateTab(tabId, { url }): Promise<void>, captureVisibleTab(windowId): Promise<string> }` plus `chromeCommandPorts(): ChromePorts` implemented over `chrome.tabs.query({ active: true, currentWindow: true })`, `chrome.scripting.executeScript`, `chrome.tabs.update`, `chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab(windowId, { format: 'png' })`. Justification for the interface: the unit tests are the real second implementation (fakes) — the service worker cannot run under vitest.

Create `src/extension/page-actions.ts` exporting `pageActionHandlers(ports: ChromePorts): Record<PageAction, Handler>` with all eight actions real: `ping` returns `{ ok: true, ts }`; the other seven copy the `case` bodies from `extension/src/background/command-handler.ts` lines ~391-485 verbatim in behaviour: readPage = `document.documentElement.outerHTML`; getPageText = `document.body.innerText`; findElement = `querySelectorAll(selector).length` → `{ found, matches }`; clickElement = `HTMLElement.click()` → `{ clicked }`; typeText = set `.value` + dispatch `input`/`change` (or `textContent` + `input` when contentEditable) → `{ typed }`; navigateTo = `updateTab(tabId, { url })`; captureTab = `captureVisibleTab(windowId)` → `{ dataUrl }`. Validate `params` with hand-written guards (selector is a non-empty string, url is a string, …) and return `{ error }` on bad params instead of throwing.

Apply `maxChars` (from params, default 200000) to readPage and getPageText results: slice and add `truncated: true, totalChars` to the result; captureTab is left uncapped here (the MCP server phase decides how to present the PNG).

Create `src/extension/service-worker.ts` wiring: start keepalive, create the dispatcher over `pageActionHandlers(chromeCommandPorts())`, create the bridge client with `onCommand = dispatcher`, `socketFactory = (url) => new WebSocket(url)`.

Unit tests with fake sockets / fake alarms / a fake `ChromePorts` (no real network, no real Chrome): bridge-client sends hello on open, routes a command to onCommand and writes the response with the same id, buffers before open, reconnects after close; keepalive creates the alarm once; dispatcher answers ping and errors on unknown action; page-actions per action — correct tabId/windowId routing, param validation errors, truncation flag and length, `findElement` zero-match shape.

Manual check recorded in the phase notes: `npm run relay` in one terminal, load `dist/extension/` unpacked in chrome://extensions, confirm the relay logs an extension `hello`, then pipe a `{"kind":"command","data":{"id":"1","action":"getPageText","params":{}}}` frame through a throwaway `ws` client (or `extension/devtools/tail-logs.mjs` with `BRIDGE_URL=ws://127.0.0.1:8766`) and confirm the active tab's text comes back.

extension/src/background/command-handler.ts (the seven page-action case bodies and the ports pattern) + extension/public/manifest.json (manifest baseline)
Relay from the previous phase for the manual connection check
phases.expectedResult: `tools/chrome-bridge/dist/extension/` (built by `npm run build:extension`) loads unpacked in Chrome, connects to the running relay, and answers page-action commands (`ping`, `getPageText`, …) on a real tab with matching `command-response` frames, with all eight handlers covered by passing fake-port unit tests.

`cat dist/extension/manifest.json` shows `"name": "Chrome Bridge"`, `manifest_version: 3`, `permissions` equal to the set {tabs, activeTab, scripting, storage, alarms} and nothing else, `host_permissions: ["<all_urls>"]`, `background.service_worker: "service-worker.js"`, `background.type: "module"`, and no `action`, `content_scripts`, or `web_accessible_resources` keys.

`grep -ciE 'provider|storyId|dashboard-|sessionState|boky' dist/extension/service-worker.js` returns 0, and `grep -rn 'extension/src' tools/chrome-bridge/src/extension tools/chrome-bridge/vite.extension.config.ts` returns nothing (no relative or alias import into boky's tree).
